title: Sunshine Act Meetings
summary:
This notice shares two updates: how the United States trade office will handle confidential business information in public comments, and what the Unified Carrier Registration Plan’s enforcement team plans to discuss at its upcoming public meeting.

First, the Office of the United States Trade Representative says that companies can submit materials with confidential business information that will not be posted publicly if they are clearly marked. At the same time, they must also submit a version that can be shared with the public. Most other attachments will be posted online for anyone to read. If a company believes these steps do not fully protect its information, it can contact the office to discuss other options. The goal is to balance transparency with the need to protect sensitive details.

Second, the Unified Carrier Registration Plan’s Enforcement Subcommittee will hold an open meeting by phone and video on October 28, 2025. The agenda includes a review of enforcement and compliance results through the third quarter of 2025, scheduling two enforcement awareness weeks in January and June 2026 to avoid holiday conflicts, discussing inspection standards for passenger carriers, expanding cooperation with more states and territories, distributing quick-reference cards for officers, and creating quarterly online training for enforcement staff to promote consistent practices.

Who benefits? Companies that comment on trade matters get clearer guidance on how to protect their sensitive data while still contributing to public debate. The public gains more access to information. In road transportation, carriers that follow the rules and the agencies that oversee them could see fairer, more consistent enforcement, better training, and stronger safety outcomes.

Who might be negatively affected? Businesses that are wary of sharing details may worry that public versions reveal more than they’d like. Smaller carriers and operators with tight resources might feel added strain from more inspections or new training and documentation expectations. Operators that are not in compliance could face increased scrutiny and penalties. Overall, these steps aim to improve transparency in trade policy and strengthen safety enforcement in a measured, public way.
